steps.body: Comparing fractions demands ONE shared whole. Half a small pizza against a quarter of a giant one compares the pizzas, not the fractions.
steps.narration: Comparing fractions demands ONE shared whole. Half a small pizza against a quarter of a giant one compares the pizzas, not the fractions.

widget.prompt: Both wholes are the same size. Build the greater of 3/8 and 5/8.
widget.successFeedback: 5/8 — five identical eighth-pieces beat three of them, because the whole is shared.
widget.lowFeedback: Your shaded bar is shorter than the target half. Shade more — raise the numerator, or use fewer parts.
widget.highFeedback: Your shaded bar is longer than half. Shade less — lower the numerator, or split into more parts.

commonFractions.feedback: 3/8 holds fewer of the very same pieces, so it is the smaller amount.
8/8 is the entire whole, which was not one of the two fractions offered.

predict.prompt: Ben's 1/4 slice is bigger than Maya's 1/2 slice. Is 1/4 > 1/2?
predict.reveal: His pizza was larger. Fraction comparison only means something when both fractions share one whole.

cml.actionGoal: Cut, count, and compare equal pieces to see what g3f same whole really names.
invariants: A fraction names equal shares of ONE whole: the denominator says how many equal pieces the whole became, and the numerator counts them, which is what makes g3f same whole comparable at all.
misconceptions: Calling unequal pieces fractions, reading the denominator as a count, or comparing fractions that came from different-sized wholes.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the whole changed size, which of these comparisons would stop being trustworthy?

widget.prompt: Maya eats 1/2 of a small pizza. Ben eats 1/4 of a giant pizza. Ben's piece is bigger. Does that mean 1/4 > 1/2?

options.label: No — the wholes were different sizes
options.feedback: Correct — fraction comparison assumes ONE shared whole; different wholes make the comparison meaningless.

options.label: Yes — Ben's piece was bigger
options.feedback: Bigger piece, yes, but from a bigger pizza; that compares the pizzas, not the fractions.

options.label: Yes — fourths are always bigger
options.feedback: Within one whole, fourths are always SMALLER than halves; more pieces means smaller pieces.

options.label: There is no way to tell
options.feedback: There is: with the same whole, 1/2 is always greater than 1/4, and that is what the symbols compare.

widget.prompt: Two identical wholes are cut into sixths. Which is greater, 4/6 or 5/6?

options.feedback: Correct — the pieces are the same size, so holding 5 of them beats holding 4.
4 pieces is fewer than 5 pieces of the very same size, so this is the smaller amount.

options.label: they are equal
options.feedback: They hold different numbers of identical sixth-size pieces, so they cannot be equal.

options.label: there is no way to tell
options.feedback: There is: the wholes match and the pieces match, so comparing the counts settles it completely.
